memoryText: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Lamentations 3:22-23 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Few verses have comforted more people in grief than this one. It is surprising because of where it appears: in the center of a book of mourning over a destroyed city.

“The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases.” The word for steadfast love, hesed, is the covenant word. It means loyal, faithful, committed love. It is the love of God that holds to the covenant even when his people have broken it. And “never ceases” means that it does not run out, even after disaster. The city has fallen, but God’s love has not. The people had been tempted to think that they had exhausted God’s patience. This verse says that his love is not a resource that can be used up.

“His mercies never come to an end.” Mercies are acts of compassion, plural, as in many small acts. They are tender, like a mother’s compassion for a child. They never come to an end. The two phrases say the same thing in two ways, as Hebrew poetry often does: God’s love and compassion are inexhaustible.

“They are new every morning.” Each day brings fresh supplies. The mercy we need for today is not leftover mercy from yesterday. It is given new. This is a daily rhythm. We do not need to carry yesterday’s failures or tomorrow’s worries, because mercy is renewed with every sunrise.

“Great is your faithfulness.” The conclusion is a statement of praise, which gives us the title of the famous hymn. Faithfulness is God’s reliability. He keeps his word. Say this verse every morning this week, as you wake. Let it set the tone for the day.
weekInReview: This week you moved from the end of Jeremiah into the exile itself. You prayed Psalm 119’s closing stanzas as the prayer of one who clings to God’s word and then confesses that he is a lost sheep, and the first two Songs of Ascents, which move from distress to the confidence that the LORD is our keeper. You read all five poems of Lamentations, which give words for grief: the weeping widow, the cry of “Is it nothing to you?”, the center that remembers God’s steadfast love, and the final plea, “Restore us to yourself, O LORD.” Then you began Ezekiel, a priest in exile, who saw the glory of God on a mobile throne in Babylon, ate a scroll that tasted sweet as honey, and was made a watchman. The week taught that grief is a form of prayer, that God’s mercy is new every morning, and that God is present even in exile.
reflectionQuestions: Lamentations gives a voice to grief. What sorrow have you not yet brought to God in prayer, and what might it look like to do so?
The hope in the center of Lamentations comes from remembering who God is. What is one truth about God’s character that has held you in a hard time?
Ezekiel saw God’s glory in a foreign land. Where do you feel far from God, and how does this vision speak to that place?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that his mercies are new every morning.
Name a way he was faithful this week.
